title: Counting Israel's Fighting Men
overview: About a year after leaving Egypt, Israel counts its men of fighting age tribe by tribe and sets the tribe of Levi apart to care for the sanctuary tent.

parts.label: The LORD orders a count (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Camped in the Sinai desert, the people are told to register every man aged twenty or older who could serve in the army, family by family. The count organizes them for the march and the battles ahead on the way to the land promised to them.

parts.label: Twelve tribal leaders named (vv. 5-16)
parts.note: Each tribe's chief helps run the count, so every tribe is represented. Joseph's descendants count as two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh, because Jacob had adopted both of Joseph's sons as his own.

parts.label: Everyone registers by family (vv. 17-19)
parts.note: The work starts the same day the order is given, with each man listed by name under his clan and household. Knowing which family you belonged to mattered for later laws about close relatives and for dividing up land.

parts.label: Tribe by tribe totals (vv. 20-43)
parts.note: Judah is the largest tribe, which fits its later role leading the march. Every total ends in hundreds, except Gad's, which ends in fifty; one older suggestion is that the men were counted through leaders already placed over groups of hundreds and fifties.

parts.label: The grand total (vv. 44-46)
parts.note: The total of 603,550 fighting men would imply a whole population of perhaps two million. Scholars debate how to understand numbers this large.

parts.label: The Levites set apart (vv. 47-54)
parts.note: Levi is not counted for the army because its job is to take down, carry, set up and guard the tabernacle, the portable tent where the LORD was believed to be present. The Levites camp around it as a buffer, and the text bluntly says any outsider who comes near is to be put to death, because careless contact with the holy was believed to bring disaster on everyone.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the very large totals are literal headcounts or whether the Hebrew word usually translated 'thousand' here means a smaller unit, such as a clan or a troop, which would make the actual numbers much lower.
think: Being counted by name can mean being known and valued, or being drafted for a burden. When has being counted felt like one of these to you, and when has it felt like the other?
